title: A pending-write queue is the single source of truth for what the server has not confirmed
context: Recording rallies while the network is poor is the case that decides this design. If the draft only advances once the server confirms, every rally costs a round trip plus retries, and in a gym with weak signal the recorder simply cannot keep up with play. Advancing optimistically fixes that, but it moves the failure somewhere the recorder cannot see: the preview card has already become the next draft, so a rally that never reached the server leaves no trace on the screen the recorder is looking at. Something has to remember what is still unconfirmed, and something has to say so where it is always visible.
decision: Unconfirmed writes live in a pending queue in its own Redux slice, holding the entry together with its attempt count and the timestamp of its next scheduled attempt. Both the header component named SyncIndicator and the per-row failure marker are pure derivations of that queue rather than stored status of their own, following the same rule this repository already adopted for statistics: a fact that can drift is derived, not stored. Empty queue reads as synced; any item with a scheduled attempt reads as syncing; a queue whose items have all exhausted their backoff reads as unsynced, with the count. The queue also owns retry scheduling — in-request attempts first, then a longer background backoff — and flushes in full whenever a new entry is enqueued, so a transient failure usually repairs itself on the next rally without the recorder doing anything.

alternatives.option: Keep the draft blocked until the server confirms, and show a delayed spinner
alternatives.reason: Correct by construction and needs no queue, but its premise is that the happy path is fast. Under sustained poor network that premise fails and recording becomes unusable — which is the situation the app is most likely to be used in.

alternatives.option: Strict FIFO send queue that holds every later entry until the current one lands
alternatives.reason: Guarantees the server is never internally inconsistent, but one permanently failing rally would hold back every rally after it. Losing twenty rallies because the fifth failed is worse than a single temporary gap that repairs itself on retry.

alternatives.option: Store the indicator state as its own field, updated by the write path
alternatives.reason: A second copy of something the queue already says, free to drift from it — and drift here means the indicator claims everything is saved while an entry sits unsent.

alternatives.option: Escalate to the failed state as soon as the in-request retries are exhausted
alternatives.reason: Alarms the recorder for something that usually repairs itself within seconds. The indicator should stay on syncing while an attempt is still scheduled and escalate only when nothing further is planned — or immediately for a 4xx, where retrying cannot help.

alternatives.option: Add SyncIndicator as a fourth flex child of the header
alternatives.reason: Measured at 375px it overflows by 37px and clips the settings button — the header's three columns already sit one pixel inside the available width.

alternatives.option: Shrink the back and settings buttons to icon size to make room
alternatives.reason: Frees enough width, but drops their tap targets from 60x36 to 32x32, further below the 44px guideline for two controls that must be hit accurately mid-match.

alternatives.option: Position SyncIndicator absolutely so it costs no layout width
alternatives.reason: Works, but there is no clean vertical space for it: below the set score only about fourteen pixels remain, so it either overlaps the score or straddles the header's bottom edge, and the hit area stays cramped either way.

alternatives.option: Render SyncIndicator only when something is pending
alternatives.reason: Contradicts the decision to keep the state always checkable, and it still overflows at precisely the moment it needs to be shown.

consequences: The optimistic advance is only defensible because three things hold together: seq keeps arrival order from deciding array order, the queue retries automatically, and the indicator makes what remains visible. Removing any one of them reopens a real failure.

SyncIndicator ships all three queue states, but it reports queue state and not connection state — offline detection and multi-device semantics remain with the synchronised-recording work, which extends this indicator rather than replacing it.
The queue sits in its own slice rather than the game slice: its lifetime differs from per-set draft state, and it is what a later Change persists.

The queue is in memory only. An app killed while entries are unconfirmed loses them, which is worse than today's behaviour in that one scenario; closing it is scoped to the follow-up that persists the queue.
The update path deliberately does not advance optimistically, so the two paths present failure differently — on the entry row for create, on the card for update.

Making room for SyncIndicator replaces the numeric set score with SetTally — per-side cells filled from the bottom, sized from the match's set count — which brings the Scores component into this Change's scope.
revisitTriggers: The queue is persisted across app restarts, at which point the residual data-loss risk recorded here is closed and this decision's consequences should be reconciled.
Connection state arrives with synchronised recording and the indicator gains a second dimension, making the current queue-only semantics worth restating.
Backoff intervals prove wrong in the field — too eager to alarm, or too slow to recover — which is a tuning change to the queue rather than a change of shape.
